# Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph

Every Mac since macOS 13 (2022) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph.

The position

A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3 , emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1 ; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. What is lost is someone else.

## Finding

What if I told you that every Mac since 2022 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe me?

Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page ( man 8 knowledgeconstructiond ), and this is all you get:

NAME knowledgeconstructiond – A daemon that analyzes content on the device to build a general purpose knowledge graph. DESCRIPTION knowledgeconstructiond analyzes the content on this device to help build a knowledge graph representing the device and the user. It works together with intelligenceplatformd, performing some of the heavy processing tasks, to generate the knowledge graph.

Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. And not a word about the "kinship" inference discussed below. Also, we personally ran into it while doing some security research on the Apple Intelligence bundle in macOS 26 in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform ; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work .

But we go a bit deeper.

This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing).

To this end, we open-source a local dashboard ( iKnow ) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac.

Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: weaponizing and exploiting. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM).

## What's in the personal knowledge graph?

The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform , a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access.

Likely, the most interesting is graph.db . It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity (a person, an app, an event); the object is either a plain value (a name, a handle, a date) or another entity, which is where the graph gets its edges. The predicate is the interesting part: it says what kind of relationship the system believes holds between the two.

One edge of the graph (synthetic data): a person and the organization the store holds as their employer. PS500 is the id predicate.json gives employer , and its range is not an organization but a relationship type — so one edge is two rows sharing a relationshipId , one naming the kind of relationship and one pointing at the other entity. The forty-six relationship type classes in the table below exist to carry exactly that, which is what lets an edge hold a confidence of its own and be retracted later.

Most of what the two daemons do is populate those predicates, and the tables kept beside them, from everything the OS will let them read. Into the graph go Contacts; Photos (faces); Calendar (titles and attendees); Family Sharing (including the age of every member); the Medical ID emergency contact in Health; events and contacts Siri Suggestions finds in Mail and Messages; people donated by apps through App Intents; and installed apps. Beside it, in tables of their own, sit who appears with whom in your photos; the communication log (who, when, which app, which direction; no content), which also pulls from your other devices; location and movement; and a long tail of device signals (screen locked, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, charging, ambient light, and a stream named ContextualUnderstanding.PhysicalSocial whose record format lists people by name, phone and email, each with a start and an end time; it reads like a log of who was physically around you, though we never saw it filled in).

## What is inferred

The complete list of the 181 entity classes:

Every class the shipped ontology declares, grouped rather than left in file order: the core types, then people, attributes, places and events, then the activity block, and last the forty-six relationship types , which are not things at all — each one reifies an edge so that the edge can carry facets of its own, a confidence among them. The ids and labels are Apple's; the grouping is ours. intValue runs 1 to 185 with four numbers missing — 18, 54, 169, 181 — and nothing on the disk says what they were.

Fifty-seven of the 181 describe an activity: sleeping , exercising , mindfulness , going to bed , commute , dining , most of them with a matching type class beside them, so nearly a third of the vocabulary went on what you are doing rather than on who or where you are. That said, it is not clear that every class is actually used; some may be placeholders that are declared and never filled. In the table, we flag as implemented the classes for which we could locate a mechanism that might be responsible for the class, but those are to be taken as inference work rather than ground truth.

And this is the complete list of predicates (same disclaimer applies):

Every predicate the shipped ontology declares. The first column is the id as graph.db stores it; the last says how a value gets there: copied from a source, joined from another record, derived by a rule, shipped by Apple as world knowledge, or produced by a model (in bold). Seven we could not establish, and the table says so rather than guessing. The ids and labels are Apple's; the plain-language readings are ours.

## How it is inferred

The methods run the whole range. Most of the vocabulary is filled by plain copying (a name from Contacts, an attendee from Calendar) and rules over the copies; the interesting rows come from models: a pair of XGBoost classifiers decides who is family from 144 mostly behavioral features, two embedding models are one of ten signals the system uses to decide when two records are the same person, twelve analyzers in Photos score partner, parent, child, coworker and friend from who appears in your pictures with you, on which trips and holidays, and Apple's on-device LLM reads your messages to put a name and a relationship on a face (if Apple Intelligence is active).

Whatever the method, every row lands in the graph with a confidence attached, a number between 0 and 1.

The family scores live apart. Two CoreML models ship next to the ontology, EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc and EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends.mlmodelc : binary XGBoost classifiers that take 144 features and return a class and a probability over it. Their scores do not go into the triple store but into a table of their own ( entityTagging.db , one row per person, seventeen relationship columns from family to mother to coworker , recomputed every day), which is what the iKnow scorecard further down reads. Only two of those seventeen columns have a shipped model behind them; what fills the other fifteen, and how any of these probabilities would become a confidence in the graph, we could not trace.

The feature names are in each model's metadata.json , in plain text. They are the clearest statement of what this system is that I have found anywhere. All 144:

Every input EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc reads, in the order its metadata.json declares them. EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends reads the same 144 in the same order, and every one is a number. The groups are the schema's own three blocks: twenty on who the person is, forty on when and how you communicate with them, eighty-four on the photographs you both appear in. Two of the twenty, photosPersonAge and photosAgeDifferenceCategory , are read from Photos too. The names are Apple's; the group labels are ours.

The identity group is the tidy story: same surname, same home address, an iCloud Family flag — and it is the small half. The bulk of the model is the other two: who you message and who appears in your photographs, conditioned on the day of the week and the time of day, and then on both at once. photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight is a shipped feature name in a shipped classifier whose job is deciding whether someone is family.

Deleting something does not delete it everywhere.

The live graph forgets. Delete a contact and nothing re-derives them; the next run replaces the table wholesale.

But the store keeps a second table, expired_stable_graph , beside the live one. The retracted row moves there and keeps its confidence and its sources. How long it stays there is not clear from what we could see. It seems to go after about 48 hours (the store keeps a prune watermark, and a recent snapshot of the table reached back no further than that); but on my own Mac, I could still read very old records in it.

And a conclusion can outlive the evidence for it. On my Mac, the scorecard still scored two people the graph had dropped the day before, both of them known to it only from a calendar invitation. Well, if you want your partner not to discover some contacts you might have deleted and their "closeness" to you, better to drop some rows from expired_stable_graph too (unfortunately, you have to do it manually). But I am sure you have nothing to hide (just joking).

# Remote code execution on Vast.ai host via cloud-sync symlink abuse

Vast.ai lets clients rent GPUs on machines run by independent hosts. We disclosed a vulnerability that allowed an attacker renting a GPU to escape their container and run code as root on the host machine. Vast.ai patched it.

Found by

- Kibitz

The position

Promotion: a pawn that reaches the eighth rank stops being a pawn. The pawn is the client's dst path, checked as a string and harmless inside their own container. The host resolves it outside the container, follows the symlink the client planted, and the path arrives as a root write. b8=Q gives check along the eighth rank and hits the knight on b4 down the b-file. The sanitizer read what the path said, not what it would become.

## Finding

## What's Vast.ai

Vast.ai is a marketplace for GPUs; essentially, the Airbnb of GPUs. A host puts GPUs up for rent: an organization or an individual with spare ones. A client rents them, by the hour. At the time of this write-up, Vast.ai manages 20,000 GPUs worldwide with 700k monthly transactions.

How it works: Vast.ai manages two main things: a client-host matching platform that handles prices, offer discovery, and the life-cycle of the renting process; and the software used on clients (APIs to the Vast.ai service) and hosts. When a client rents a GPU through the Vast.ai service, a Docker container is spawned inside the host machine and the GPUs the client is paying for are bound to the container exclusively. The client gets an SSH channel to the container, which they use to carry out the needed computation on the GPU. This process on the host is managed by a daemon (kaalia) provided by Vast.ai, which runs at the highest privilege within the host machine and communicates directly with the Vast.ai servers.

The client talks to Vast.ai to rent and to the container to work. Vast.ai reaches the host machine through kaalia, on a connection kaalia opened.

kaalia is Vast.ai's software. It runs with the highest privilege on the host machine, where it manages the containers.

We found a vulnerability that allowed a malicious client to achieve root-level arbitrary write and so root-level remote code execution on host machines the client was renting a GPU on. Meaning: a malicious client could rent a GPU on a given host, run the exploit to escape the container assigned to them, and achieve root code execution on the host machine. The vulnerability has been fully patched.

## The vulnerability

The Vast.ai system provides additional capabilities besides spawning containers on the host's machine. One of these is Cloud Sync . Its purpose is to allow clients to copy files between the file system of the rented container and their own cloud storage (e.g., an AWS bucket), in either direction. Everything below concerns the Cloud To Instance direction.

A copy is one API call that gets two main inputs: the source file to copy from, and a destination path, i.e., where in the client's container to copy the source; for instance:

{ "transfer": "Cloud To Instance", "src": "mybucket:datasets/train.tar", "dst": "/workspace/data", "instance_id": 8675309 } pull an object from your own bucket down into the instance you rented. the files land at dst, inside the instance.

Now, the thing is that, on the host machine, the code that takes care of the copy does not run within the client's container. It runs as part of a daemon and within the host machine's file system. What happens is that the daemon spawns a Python process that runs rclone which creates the destination path by merging the dst path with the appropriate prefix to reach the writable layer of the client's container, e.g., /var/lib/docker/overlay2/<id>/diff/ . The process summarized:

The client never speaks to kaalia. The host machine dials out and the control plane pushes it a task; everything after that happens on the host machine.

The code that performs the copy is fetched by the daemon at task time.

The destination path was sanitized: .. , quotes, and shell metacharacters were all rejected. Symlinks were not. So, how we exploited this: we created a destination path that pointed to a symlink into the container's file system (recall: the client has SSH on the container running on the host), in turn, the symlink pointed to a path that resolved into the host file, e.g.,

$ ln -sfn /var/lib/vastai_kaalia /root/vpdst $ ls -la /root/vpdst lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 24 /root/vpdst -> /var/lib/vastai_kaalia

The host followed the link out of the container, allowing a write into the directory it pointed to:

The client wrote the link from inside. The host followed it from outside. Same inode, two namespaces, and the only one that got consulted was the one the client was not in.

Now, because rclone is executed as part of the daemon running on the host, it has root privileges; therefore, the one above was an arbitrary write with root privileges primitive . An arbitrary root write is not yet code execution. On a Vast.ai host, the step from one to the other was a root cron job. update_scripts.sh puts four entries in root's crontab, and one of them is:

*/5 * * * * python3 /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/read_packs.py # the interpreter is named on the command line, so the file's mode and owner # do not matter. Only the contents do — and a copy overwrites contents.

So an attacker could point the write at /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/read_packs.py , copy their own Python over it (e.g., a reverse shell), and within five minutes root would run it. That is root code execution on the host.

## Other findings

During the game with Vast.ai, we could locate an additional critical vulnerability with equivalent impact to the abuse of rclone above but that required a man-in-the-middle attacker:

### Vast.ai-to-host communication could be downgraded to be plain-text (and get root code execution on host to a MitM)

An attacker who sat on the network path between a host and Vast.ai's control plane could run commands as root on that host, with no Vast.ai account, no rented instance, and nothing to break in the cryptography.

The daemon we tested (version 303) set TLS up correctly — it loaded the CA bundle, verified the certificate, and pinned both the hostname and the peer's IP, so a forged certificate was refused. The defect was in the caller: when the TLS connection failed, the daemon retried the same connection in cleartext and logged TLS connect failed; falling back to cleartext . The attacker never had to touch the certificate. They made the handshake fail (a dropped packet, a TCP reset) and answered the cleartext connection that followed. Nothing under the transport authenticated the peer, so a single-element Command on that link went straight to /bin/sh -c as the daemon's account, which has sudo .

TLS was never broken. The daemon dropped it whenever a handshake failed, and the attacker decided when a handshake failed.

The attacker needed no Vast.ai account and no rental, only a place on the path. Everything down to /bin/sh -c was run against daemon 303 in an airgapped lab. The last leg is drawn dashed: the step from that account to root was deliberately not run.

We thank the Vast.ai team for the flawless collaboration and handling of the reported vulnerabilities.
